explanations.explanation: This neuron fires on tokens that mark document‐ or code‐level headings and metadata—section titles, file‐header comments (e.g. copyright/license blocks), markdown headings, XML declarations, etc.—essentially signals structural “header” elements rather than ordinary prose.
This neuron is essentially a sub‐word-prefix detector: it lights up on the first BPE piece of longer words (common prefixes or name initials) rather than on standalone short words.

This head appears to be a “discourse‐marker” detector—it lights up on single words that structure or qualify a statement (intensifiers like truly, concessives like albeit/whereas, reporting cues like mentioned, category labels like positives, directional or descriptive tags like southeast or ghostly, etc.). In other words, it flags content words whose main role is to signal emphasis, contrast, or framing in the discourse.

This neuron fires on the “pivot” of a phrase—the single token that names or points to the main topic or entity under discussion.  Whether it’s the head noun or adjective in a scientific title (hippocampal), a demonstrative pronoun in Japanese (これ), the first character of “necessary”/“must” (必 in 必要/必须), or a key metadata field in code or markup (description), it consistently marks the token that carries the phrase’s central referential load.

This feature is simply a subword‐level detector for the letter sequence “scr” (as in words like scrambling, scratches, scrambling, riffling, etc.), i.e. it flags tokens that begin with the orthographic trigram “scr.”

This feature fires on structural markup tokens that signal “non-prose” elements—e.g. Markdown image links with attributes, import-from code snippets, Q:/A: or Hint: labels, and LaTeX/math delimiters—i.e. the scaffolding of questions, answers, code blocks and formulas rather than ordinary running text.

This neuron lights up on sentence‐ or clause-initial connective/anaphoric words that tie back to prior content—e.g. “Which…,” “Both…,” “Those…,” “Old…,” “Gent(lemen)….” It flags discourse markers and referential heads that launch follow-on comments, summaries or relative clauses.
This neuron fires on superlative recency markers—i.e. the adjective “newest” (and to a lesser extent synonyms like “latest”) that flag something as the most recent or up-to-date item.

This feature reliably flags the orthographic prefix “pre-” (meaning “before”) in English compounds—e.g. preface, predawn, pre–service, prefecture, preborn, preexisting—by detecting the letters p-r-e at the start of such morphemes.
This neuron is a “morphological‐prefix” detector – it spikes on the very first subword of content words, especially common English (and chemical/Arabic) prefixes (un-, di-, be-, pro-, Al-, etc.).
